Short answer: they disagree on all three levels. The clearest standards text, RFC 9309, says robots.txt contains rules crawlers are “requested to honor” and that those rules “are not a form of access authorization,” which supports the “preference/advisory” view rather than the “permission” view. (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309)

**Supported fact**

Standards participants do not speak with one voice. RFC 9309 defines robots.txt as a protocol for crawler behavior and expressly says it is not access authorization. (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309) Google’s documentation is similar: it says robots.txt is mainly for managing crawler traffic, “cannot enforce crawler behavior,” is not a way to keep pages out of Google by itself, and disallowed URLs can still appear in search results. (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) The W3C Community Group’s TDM Reservation Protocol instead defines a separate protocol “capable of expressing the reservation of rights” for text and data mining under EU copyright law, and its status page says it is not a W3C Standard. (https://www.w3.org/community/reports/tdmrep/CG-FINAL-tdmrep-20240510/) The same W3C Community Group later wrote that using robots.txt as a search opt-in is only a “complementary solution,” that this complementarity “remains subject to interpretation,” and that a more explicit signal could be more secure. (https://www.w3.org/community/tdmrep/) Meanwhile, an active IETF draft proposes updating RFC 9309 so robots.txt can carry “usage preferences,” and EDRLab’s notes from the IETF AI-Pref meeting say the presence of an AI-Pref signal in robots.txt is “logically sufficient to express a reservation of rights” under EU CDSM Article 4. (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-attach/05/ ; https://www.edrlab.org/2026/04/17/notes-from-the-ietf-ai-pref-toronto-meeting-april-2026/) The European Commission’s 1 December 2025 consultation page says the GPAI Code of Practice

Short answer: they disagree on all three levels. The clearest standards text, RFC 9309, says robots.txt contains rules crawlers are “requested to honor” and that those rules “are not a form of access authorization,” which supports the “preference/advisory” view rather than the “permission” view. (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309)

**Supported fact**

Standards participants do not speak with one voice. RFC 9309 defines robots.txt as a protocol for crawler behavior and expressly says it is not access authorization. (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309) Google’s documentation is similar: it says robots.txt is mainly for managing crawler traffic, “cannot enforce crawler behavior,” is not a way to keep pages out of Google by itself, and disallowed URLs can still appear in search results. (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) The W3C Community Group’s TDM Reservation Protocol instead defines a separate protocol “capable of expressing the reservation of rights” for text and data mining under EU copyright law, and its status page says it is not a W3C Standard. (https://www.w3.org/community/reports/tdmrep/CG-FINAL-tdmrep-20240510/) The same W3C Community Group later wrote that using robots.txt as a search opt-in is only a “complementary solution,” that this complementarity “remains subject to interpretation,” and that a more explicit signal could be more secure. (https://www.w3.org/community/tdmrep/) Meanwhile, an active IETF draft proposes updating RFC 9309 so robots.txt can carry “usage preferences,” and EDRLab’s notes from the IETF AI-Pref meeting say the presence of an AI-Pref signal in robots.txt is “logically sufficient to express a reservation of rights” under EU CDSM Article 4. (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-attach/05/ ; https://www.edrlab.org/2026/04/17/notes-from-the-ietf-ai-pref-toronto-meeting-april-2026/) The European Commission’s 1 December 2025 consultation page says the GPAI Code of Practice includes both a commitment to respect robots.txt and a commitment to identify and comply with additional machine-readable rights-reservation protocols. (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/commission-launches-consultation-protocols-reserving-rights-text-and-data-mining-under-ai-act-and)

Crawler operators also use mixed language. Google says its common crawlers “always obey robots.txt rules when crawling automatically,” and its `Google-Extended` token lets publishers manage whether crawled content may be used for Gemini training and grounding. (https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers) OpenAI says publishers may need to update robots.txt so `OAI-SearchBot` has access, says `GPTBot` disallowance indicates content should not be used for training, and says some user-initiated `ChatGPT-User` fetches may fall outside normal robots.txt application. (https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12627856-publishers-and-developers-faq ; https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots) OpenAI’s advertiser guidance is even stronger permission language: it says robots.txt tells crawlers whether they are “permitted” to access parts of a site and that crawling stops if access is disallowed. (https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001243-advertiser-guidance-for-allowing-openai-web-crawlers) Anthropic says its bots honor robots.txt, respect anti-circumvention measures, support `Crawl-delay`, and require robots.txt changes for opt-out because IP blocking can interfere with the bot’s ability to read robots.txt. (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8896518-does-anthropic-crawl-data-from-the-web-and-how-can-site-owners-block-the-crawler) Common Crawl says `CCBot` obeys `Crawl-delay`, can be blocked with robots.txt, encourages publishers to use robots.txt to control crawling, and separately says it will continue to process legal requests. (https://commoncrawl.org/faq ; https://commoncrawl.org/ccbot ; https://commoncrawl.org/blog/common-crawl-foundation-opt-out-registry)

Publishers are split too. Medium’s official blog says bots crawl public-web content by default, describes robots.txt as the place where Medium tells bots what they are and are not allowed to crawl, and frames search crawling as a trade of consent, credit, and compensation. (https://medium.com/blog/how-and-when-does-your-writing-show-up-inside-ai-chatbots-1d2dec42f26d) But the same Medium post also says robots.txt “isn’t a legally binding arrangement,” is a “voluntary technical standard,” and depends on actors respecting it. (https://medium.com/blog/how-and-when-does-your-writing-show-up-inside-ai-chatbots-1d2dec42f26d) On the other hand, the RSL guidance shows a publisher-oriented attempt to use robots.txt as a pointer to enforceable licensing terms: one example robots.txt file links to a `license.xml` and says AI training is prohibited unless permission is obtained through licensing and compensation terms. (https://rslstandard.org/guide/ai-preferences)

Courts have also not reduced robots.txt to one stable legal meaning. In `eBay v. Bidder’s Edge`, the court issued a preliminary injunction against automated crawling, and the summary says the site’s being publicly accessible did not make the crawling authorized because eBay did not permit that type of automated access without express permission. (https://www.internetlibrary.com/cases/lib_case249.cfm) In `hiQ v. LinkedIn`, by contrast, the Ninth Circuit said public websites have no relevant “gates” in their publicly available sections and concluded that the CFAA concept of access “without authorization” does not apply to public websites. (https://files.passle.net/Passle/65737bea961a63814fd9b845/MediaLibrary/Images/2025-06-27-13-55-16-799-685ea2c49e19c98bad0f4ebf.pdf)

**Inference from those sources**

The disagreement is not just semantic. One camp treats robots.txt as a machine-readable statement of crawler-specific permission: that is how many publisher and crawler-operator docs describe `Allow`, `Disallow`, and bot-specific opt-outs or opt-ins. (Inference from: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001243-advertiser-guidance-for-allowing-openai-web-crawlers ; https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers ; https://medium.com/blog/how-and-when-does-your-writing-show-up-inside-ai-chatbots-1d2dec42f26d) A second camp treats it as only an advisory preference signal, because the core RFC denies that it is authorization and major search guidance denies that it enforces behavior or securely controls indexing. (Inference from: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309 ; https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) A third camp tries to give robots.txt legal significance, especially for AI and copyright, by combining it with rights-reservation vocabularies, linked licenses, or EU opt-out frameworks. (Inference from: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-attach/05/ ; https://www.edrlab.org/2026/04/17/notes-from-the-ietf-ai-pref-toronto-meeting-april-2026/ ; https://rslstandard.org/guide/ai-preferences ; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/commission-launches-consultation-protocols-reserving-rights-text-and-data-mining-under-ai-act-and)

**Uncertainty and lack of good evidence**

There is good evidence of disagreement, but not good evidence of a universal rule that robots.txt alone either grants permission or creates binding legal duties everywhere. RFC 9309 rejects the authorization reading; the W3C TDMRep group says complementarity with search remains subject to interpretation; the IETF AI-Pref work is still a draft; TDMRep is not on the W3C standards track; and the Commission was still consulting stakeholders in December 2025 on which machine-readable protocols should count. (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309 ; https://www.w3.org/community/tdmrep/ ; https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-attach/05/ ; https://www.w3.org/community/reports/tdmrep/CG-FINAL-tdmrep-20240510/ ; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/commission-launches-consultation-protocols-reserving-rights-text-and-data-mining-under-ai-act-and) The case law in the sources also cuts both ways: `eBay` supports legal consequences for unwanted scraping on one theory, while `hiQ` rejects turning access to a public website into CFAA “authorization” in the first place. (https://www.internetlibrary.com/cases/lib_case249.cfm ; https://files.passle.net/Passle/65737bea961a63814fd9b845/MediaLibrary/Images/2025-06-27-13-55-16-799-685ea2c49e19c98bad0f4ebf.pdf)

Net result: standards documents mostly anchor robots.txt in the “preferences for compliant crawlers” model, crawler operators often market it as a practical permission-control interface, and some publishers and standards participants are trying to push it toward copyright reservation and licensing, but the legal status remains fragmented and jurisdiction-specific. # Nature of Robots Exclusion Protocol Rules

According to RFC 9309, the rules have the following characteristics:

**Not Access Authorization:**
"These rules are not a form of access authorization." (Section 1.3)

**Not a Security Substitute:**
"The Robots Exclusion Protocol is not a substitute for valid content security measures." (Section 3)

The specification describes that "crawlers are requested to honor when accessing URIs" (Section 1.3), framing the rules as guidance rather than mandatory enforcement.

**Security Concern - Path Disclosure:**
"Listing paths in the robots.txt file exposes them publicly and thus makes the paths discoverable." (Section 3)

# Paper Summary: "The Liabilities of Robots.txt"

**Authors:** Chien-yi Chang and Xin He

**Core Argument:**

The paper challenges the traditional view of robots.txt as merely a voluntary guideline. With the surge in AI-driven web scraping, the authors contend that violating robots.txt directives should carry legal consequences through civil law frameworks rather than criminal or copyright approaches.

**Key Legal Claims:**

The researchers propose that robots.txt violations can establish liability under two civil doctrines in common law jurisdictions:

1. **Contract theory** — robots.txt could constitute a unilateral contract binding those who access a website
2. **Tort law** — violations might trigger liability for trespass to chattels or negligence, particularly when "notice" of restrictions exists

**Central Thesis:**

The authors argue that clarifying robots.txt liability is essential to address internet fragmentation. They contend that a balanced civil framework can preserve the internet's cooperative character while maintaining accountability in the AI era, positioning robots.txt as a viable governance tool rather than an ignored convention.

## Réponse courte

Il n'existe **aucun consensus** : la norme technique elle‑même dit explicitement que robots.txt n'est *pas* une autorisation d'accès, plusieurs éditeurs et juristes tentent de lui faire produire des effets juridiques (contrat, réserve de droits, licence), certains opérateurs de crawlers le traitent comme un simple usage de politesse non contraignant, et les participants aux standards ont délibérément exclu l'exécution/la contrainte de leur mandat. Les tribunaux, eux, ont surtout donné du poids juridique à **l'absence** de robots.txt (licence implicite) plutôt qu'à sa présence.

---

## 1. Ce que dit la norme elle‑même (fait établi, source primaire)

Le RFC 9309 (2022) est net sur les trois points de la question :

- « These rules are not a form of access authorization » (§1.3) — les règles ne sont **pas** une forme d'autorisation d'accès ; le texte parle de règles que les crawlers « are requested to honor ».
- « The Robots Exclusion Protocol is not a substitute for valid content security measures » (§3).
- Le RFC ne dit rien d'une quelconque portée juridique.

Autrement dit, la position officielle du standard est celle de la **préférence exprimée**, pas de la permission opposable. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html), [datatracker.ietf.org](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309))

Point de vocabulaire souvent confondu dans le débat public : « ne pas être une autorisation d'accès » ne signifie pas « ne produire aucun effet juridique ». Le RFC tranche la première question, pas la seconde — *c'est une lecture de ma part*, mais elle explique une grande partie du dialogue de sourds décrit ci‑dessous.

## 2. Les participants aux standards : préférence oui, contrainte hors périmètre

Le groupe de travail **AIPREF** de l'IETF a été créé pour normaliser l'expression de « preferences about how content is collected and processed » pour l'IA, en s'appuyant notamment sur le Robots Exclusion Protocol comme point d'accroche. Sa charte place explicitement « technical enforcement of preferences » **hors périmètre**. ([datatracker.ietf.org](https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/aipref/about/))

Le constat de départ des participants est que les signaux actuels « aren't working » (Mark Nottingham, cité par The Register), et que le pari est celui de l'adhésion volontaire des opérateurs. ([theregister.com](https://www.theregister.com/2025/04/09/ietf_ai_preferences_working_group/))

Les désaccords internes portent moins sur « permission vs préférence » que sur des questions non résolues : comment interpréter **l'absence de signal**, comment combiner des signaux contradictoires. ([techpolicy.press](https://www.techpolicy.press/robotstxt-is-having-a-moment-heres-why-we-should-care/)) Une analyse d'Open Future indique que les travaux « largely stalled since the summer », le brouillon de vocabulaire ne comportant que deux termes définis, dont aucun ne fait l'objet d'un accord. ([openfuture.eu](https://openfuture.eu/blog/laion-round-2-machine-readable-but-still-not-actionable/)) — *à noter : source militante/partie prenante, à lire comme un point de vue étayé plutôt que comme un compte rendu neutre.*

## 3. Les éditeurs et intermédiaires : tenter de transformer la préférence en effet juridique

C'est ici que se situe le désaccord le plus vif. Trois stratégies documentées :

**a) La réserve de droits (UE).** La *Content Signals Policy* de Cloudflare (sept. 2025) ajoute à robots.txt des signaux `search`, `ai-input`, `ai-train`, accompagnés d'une mention en majuscules : « ANY RESTRICTIONS EXPRESSED VIA CONTENT SIGNALS ARE EXPRESS RESERVATIONS OF RIGHTS UNDER ARTICLE 4 OF THE EUROPEAN UNION DIRECTIVE 2019/790… ». Mais Cloudflare maintient simultanément que ces signaux « express preferences; they are not technical countermeasures against scraping » et reconnaît que certaines entreprises les ignoreront. ([blog.cloudflare.com](https://blog.cloudflare.com/content-signals-policy/), [cloudflare.com](https://www.cloudflare.com/press/press-releases/2025/cloudflare-gives-creators-new-tool-to-control-use-of-their-content/)) La position est donc hybride assumée : préférence sur le plan technique, acte juridique sur le plan du droit d'auteur européen.

**b) La licence.** Le standard **RSL (Really Simple Licensing)**, lancé le 10 septembre 2025, dépasse le oui/non de robots.txt en y attachant des termes de licence et de redevance lisibles par machine (pay‑per‑crawl, pay‑per‑inference). ([rslstandard.org](https://rslstandard.org/), [searchengineland.com](https://searchengineland.com/really-simple-licensing-461834), [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Really_Simple_Licensing)) *Incertitude* : je n'ai pas trouvé de décision judiciaire testant l'opposabilité de termes RSL ; l'efficacité repose pour l'instant sur la coopération.

**c) La doctrine juridique.** L'article « The Liabilities of Robots.txt » (Chang & He, accepté au *Computer Law and Security Review*) conteste frontalement la vision « simple ligne directrice volontaire » et soutient qu'une violation peut engager la responsabilité civile, soit par contrat unilatéral, soit par *trespass to chattels* / négligence, la publication de robots.txt valant **notice**. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06035)) C'est une thèse académique, non un état du droit positif.

## 4. Les opérateurs de crawlers : de la déférence à la requalification

- **Perplexity**, après l'accusation de « stealth crawling » par Cloudflare (août 2025), a répondu en distinguant *agents* et *bots* : une récupération de page effectuée à la demande d'un utilisateur humain relèverait de la navigation, pas du crawl, et n'aurait donc pas à honorer robots.txt. Selon la couverture disponible, Perplexity n'a pas déclaré traiter robots.txt comme contraignant pour ce type d'accès. ([searchengineworld.com](https://www.searchengineworld.com/perplexity-responds-to-cloudflare), [cyberscoop.com](https://cyberscoop.com/perplexity-blocks-on-crawlers-cloudflare/), [ppc.land](https://ppc.land/perplexity-denies-training-ai-models-as-cloudflare-documents-stealth-crawlers/)) — *je n'ai pas pu accéder au billet de blog de Perplexity lui‑même (403), donc ces formulations sont rapportées par des tiers ; à traiter comme fiable sur la substance, prudent sur les citations exactes.*
- **Internet Archive** conteste depuis 2017 la pertinence même de l'outil pour un archiveur : robots.txt est « geared toward search engines » et ses effets rétroactifs (rachat de domaine effaçant l'historique) contredisent la mission d'archivage. L'Archive a cessé de l'honorer dans certains cas, en offrant un canal de retrait alternatif. ([blog.archive.org](https://blog.archive.org/2017/04/17/robots-txt-meant-for-search-engines-dont-work-well-for-web-archives/))

Un désaccord de fond apparaît ici : pour les éditeurs, robots.txt exprime une volonté qui devrait suivre le contenu ; pour ces opérateurs, il exprime une préférence **contextuelle** (destinée aux moteurs de recherche) qu'on peut légitimement ne pas transposer à d'autres usages.

## 5. Ce que les tribunaux ont réellement dit

*C'est le point où le débat public est le plus imprécis.* Éléments soutenus :

- **Field v. Google** (D. Nev. 2006) : le fait de **ne pas** avoir utilisé les mécanismes d'exclusion, alors que l'auteur les connaissait, a été retenu comme fondant une **licence implicite** au profit de Google. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_v._Google,_Inc.), [fairuse.stanford.edu](https://fairuse.stanford.edu/case/field-v-google-inc)) La portée juridique reconnue est donc celle du **silence**, pas celle de l'interdiction.
- **hiQ v. LinkedIn** : le Ninth Circuit a jugé que le CFAA ne s'appliquait pas au scraping de données publiquement accessibles ; l'affaire s'est ensuite soldée par un règlement défavorable à hiQ (dommages, destruction des données). ([cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/04/18/17-16783.pdf), [loeb.com](https://www.loeb.com/en/insights/publications/2022/05/ninth-circuit-provides-path-forward-for-web-scraping-of-public-data)) *Réserve* : plusieurs sources secondaires présentent cette affaire comme « robots.txt n'est pas illégal à ignorer » ; le litige portait en réalité sur des blocages techniques et une mise en demeure. Je considère l'extrapolation directe à robots.txt comme **non établie**.
- **Reddit v. Perplexity** (SDNY, oct. 2025) : Reddit avait mis en demeure Perplexity de respecter robots.txt dès mai 2024, mais les demandes en justice reposent sur le §1201 DMCA (contournement), l'enrichissement sans cause et la concurrence déloyale — **pas** sur la violation de robots.txt comme telle. ([natlawreview.com](https://natlawreview.com/article/anti-circumvention-reddits-case-against-perplexity), [forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/anishasircar/2025/10/23/would-be-bank-robbers-reddit-escalates-ai-data-wars-with-perplexity-lawsuit/)) *Inférence* : les plaignants contournent le terrain de robots.txt précisément parce que son statut juridique est incertain.
- **Kneschke v. LAION (Allemagne)** : le tribunal de première instance (LG Hamburg, 2024) avait suggéré qu'une réserve en langue naturelle pouvait être « lisible par machine » ; en appel (OLG Hamburg, déc. 2025), cette approche a été rejetée — la lisibilité par machine suppose que la réserve puisse être exploitée automatiquement, ce qui renvoie vers des mécanismes comme robots.txt, X‑Robots‑Tag ou le TDM Reservation Protocol. ([openfuture.eu](https://openfuture.eu/blog/laion-round-2-machine-readable-but-still-not-actionable/), [ipkitten.blogspot.com](https://ipkitten.blogspot.com/2024/09/guest-post-german-court-finds-laions.html), [insidetechlaw.com](https://www.insidetechlaw.com/blog/2025/12/machine-readable-opt-outs-and-ai-training-hamburg-court-clarifies-copyright-exceptions)) C'est, en l'état, **le rattachement juridique le plus solide** de robots.txt : en droit européen, il devient un véhicule privilégié de la réserve de l'article 4(3) de la directive 2019/790. *Réserve* : je n'ai pas pu ouvrir l'analyse Bird & Bird (402) et je n'ai pas lu la décision elle‑même ; la description repose sur des commentaires de cabinets et de think tanks concordants.

| AIPREF | un point d'attache pour des **préférences** ; contrainte hors périmètre ([datatracker.ietf.org](https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/aipref/about/)) |
| Cloudflare | préférence technique **+** réserve expresse de droits (UE) ([blog.cloudflare.com](https://blog.cloudflare.com/content-signals-policy/)) |

| Doctrine (Chang & He) | source possible de **responsabilité civile** ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06035)) |
| Perplexity | non contraignant pour les agents pilotés par un utilisateur ([searchengineworld.com](https://www.searchengineworld.com/perplexity-responds-to-cloudflare)) |
